meta.descriptionEn: On the night of November 13, 1985, a small eruption on a snow-capped Colombian volcano sent walls of mud racing down river valleys toward a sleeping farming town. Scientists had seen signs for months. Hazard maps existed. A report had been delivered weeks earlier. So why did more than 23,000 people never get the warning that could have saved them? This documentary follows the volcano called the Sleeping Lion, the town built on old mudflow ground, the storm that silenced the radios, and the girl whose story the world watched. Discover how one of history's deadliest lahars happened, who was blamed, and how monitoring and disaster planning changed forever.
meta.descriptionUr: 13 November 1985 ki raat Colombia ke ek barf posh volcano Nevado del Ruiz mein chhota sa dhamaka hua aur pighli hui barf ne keechar ke tufan ki shakal le li. Yeh tufan Armero naam ke soye hue shehar par toot pada. Scientists mahino se khatre ki nishaniyan dekh rahe the, hazard map bhi bana chuka tha, phir bhi hazaron log bekhabar rahe. Is documentary mein dekhein ke warning kyun nazar andaz hui, tufani raat mein kya hua, Omayra Sanchez ki kahani ne duniya ko kaise hila diya, aur is hadse ke baad volcano monitoring hamesha ke liye kaise badal gayi.

articleEn: It was the night of 13 November 1985 in Armero, Colombia. Heavy rain was falling, and people were inside their homes. At about 11:30 p.m., a huge flood of mud and rock came down from the mountain. This is called a lahar, and it swallowed the town. About 23,000 people lost their lives that night. A prosperous farming town was buried under mud, in what remains the worst natural disaster in Colombia's history.

The most painful part is that the disaster did not come without warning. Scientists had sounded the alarm months earlier. So why was the warning not acted on? How could a small eruption cause such a huge disaster? And what did Colombia change afterwards?

In this story we look for answers step by step. We will see what the mountain was like, where the town was built, and which signs were ignored. Then we will go through the full account of the night of 13 November, the story of Omayra Sánchez, and the lessons that still matter today. So let's begin a little before that night, with the long story of the mountain itself.

articleEn: Nevado del Ruiz sits on the border of two Colombian departments, Caldas and Tolima, and is the highest point in both. It lies about 130 kilometres west of the capital, Bogotá. Scientists call it a stratovolcano, a mountain built from many layers of lava, with hardened ash and other rock between them. It is part of the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the Nazca Plate moves east beneath the South American plate, and this process creates the volcanoes of the Andes.

Ruiz belongs to the Ruiz–Tolima massif, a group of five snow-capped volcanoes. Its summit carries glaciers, which is why "nevado" means "covered with snow." The history of these glaciers is striking. Between 28,000 and 21,000 years ago, ice covered about 1,500 square kilometres of the massif. By 1959 it had shrunk to 34 square kilometres, and by 2003 the ice on Nevado del Ruiz covered about 10 square kilometres. Its meltwater supplies fresh water to forty nearby towns, so its disappearance worries the people who live there.

The area lies inside Los Nevados National Natural Park. Dense forests cover the lower slopes, and the trees thin out higher up. Animals such as the mountain tapir and the spectacled bear live here, and both are classed as threatened. Twenty-seven of Colombia's endemic bird species are found here too.

Beneath this beauty, though, an old fire sleeps. According to scientists, volcanic activity here began about two million years ago and has had three major eruptive periods. The current one began about 150,000 years ago and built today's volcanic cone. In the last 11,000 years the volcano has gone through at least 12 eruption stages. In Colombia only Galeras is considered more active.

Its last big eruption before 1985 was more than 140 years earlier, so locals called it the Sleeping Lion. But the lion was sleeping, not dead. And at its foot a town had grown up, one whose own past was tied to the same mud.

articleEn: Armero was about 48 kilometres from Nevado del Ruiz and 169 kilometres from Bogotá. It was the third-largest city in Tolima and a well-known farming town. About a fifth of Colombia's rice production came from here, and it also played a big part in cotton, sorghum and coffee. Part of this prosperity came from the mountain itself, because volcanic soil is very fertile. The mountain that fed the town was also its danger.

The ground under the town carried its own record of danger. Armero was built on an alluvial fan, and that land had seen lahars pass over it before. On 13 November 1595, three Plinian eruptions took place. Their sound was heard about 100 kilometres away, and ash darkened the surrounding area. A big earthquake had struck three days before the eruptions. Lahars then ran down the valleys of the Gualí and Lagunillas rivers, and more than 600 people died. One source puts the toll at 636.

On 19 February 1845, after an earthquake, a mudflow travelled about 70 kilometres down the Lagunillas River valley. It is estimated to have killed about 1,000 people. So the danger to Armero was nothing new, and history had already written it down.

What exactly is a lahar? It is a flowing slurry of water, volcanic ash and rock, usually running down a river valley. Small lahars move at a few metres per second, while large ones can reach several tens of metres per second, and a person cannot run that fast. How does a lahar form? When pyroclastic flows melt the snow and glaciers on a summit, a great deal of water mixes with rock and ash.

One dangerous feature of a lahar is that its behaviour can change within a single event. At times it is like ordinary water, and at times like thick rubble. Such lahars can travel 100 kilometres along river valleys, and the journey can take only a few hours. On Ruiz the danger is great because there is still a large amount of ice on the summit, so even a small eruption can send a lahar down. That is what happened in 1985. In the next chapters we will see how many warning signs appeared before that night, and how they were ignored.

articleEn: In November 1984, geologists saw seismic activity rising around Nevado del Ruiz, often the first sign of an approaching eruption. Fumarole activity then increased, sulfur began to build up at the summit, and small phreatic eruptions occurred. In these, hot magma meets water and produces a steam explosion. The most notable came on 11 September 1985, when the volcano released ash. In October the activity eased somewhat.

During that time an Italian volcanological mission took gas samples from the fumaroles of the Arenas crater. They contained carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, which meant that magma was releasing gas directly into the surface environment. A report dated 22 October 1985 described the lahar danger as very high, and it also proposed some simple preparations for local authorities. Another team provided seismographs but gave no instructions on how to operate them.

A hazard map was also ready in October. It showed ash and rock danger near Murillo, Santa Isabel and Líbano, and a clear lahar threat for Mariquita, Guayabal, Chinchiná and Armero. But the map did not properly reach the people most at risk. Many survivors later said they had never heard of it, even though versions of it were printed in several major newspapers.

According to Henry Villegas of INGEOMINAS, the map clearly showed that Armero would lie in the path of lahars. But it faced strong opposition from economic interests. He also said the map was not prepared long before the eruption, so printing and distributing it in large numbers in time was difficult. There was another problem too. The map printed in Bogotá's newspaper El Espectador had serious errors. The scale was wrong, and the outer limit of the lahars was not shown. It used many colours but had no key. Armero was in the green zone, which was wrongly taken to be the safest area.

Meanwhile the Colombian Congress accused the scientific and civil defense agencies of scaremongering, so the people speaking about the danger were the ones being criticised. Armero's mayor, Ramon Rodriguez, had been appealing for months to many officials, including congressmen and the governor of Tolima. He called the volcano a time bomb and believed an eruption would break a natural dam above Armero and cause a flood. But only one congressman asked about the situation. Ministers' reports kept saying that the government was aware of the danger and working to protect the population.
The signs were there. Was the danger only kept on paper? Then 13 November arrived, and everything was about to change.

articleEn: At about 3 p.m. on 13 November 1985, columns of black ash began rising from Ruiz. The local civil defense director was informed at once. He contacted INGEOMINAS, which decided that the area should be evacuated. He was then told to talk to the civil defense directors of Bogotá and Tolima. So the question of evacuation had been raised.

Between 5 and 7 p.m. the ash stopped falling. At that time local officials, including the town priest, were telling people to stay calm and go indoors. Survivors of Armero described the night as quiet. Ash had fallen all day, and people had been told there was nothing to worry about. An emergency committee meeting was called at 5 p.m. and ended at 7 p.m. Some members then discussed evacuating Armero, Mariquita and Honda with the regional Red Cross. The Red Cross in Ibagué ordered Armero's authorities to evacuate. But because of the storm there were power problems, and the order could not be carried out.

The heavy rain and thunder of the storm may have drowned out the sound of the volcano. There was also no system for warning people in an organised way. Then the power suddenly went out and the radios fell silent. That night Armero was surrounded by darkness and rain.

When did the volcano actually erupt with a big blast? Here the sources disagree on the time. One source says the eruption happened at 3:06 p.m., while two sources give 9:09 p.m. The date is the same: 13 November 1985. In this blast, dacitic tephra reached more than 30 kilometres into the air. The total material ejected, including magma, was about 35 million tonnes. That was only 3 percent of what Mount St. Helens ejected in 1980. The eruption rated 3 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, so it was not a very large one. But it also released about 700,000 tonnes of sulfur dioxide, which is why it is called unusually sulfur-rich.

Pyroclastic flows melted the ice and glaciers on the summit. This produced four thick lahars that ran down the river valleys on the volcano's slopes. A small lake had been seen in the Arenas crater a few months earlier. It was destroyed in the eruption, and its hot, acidic water sped up the melting of the ice. The lahars contained large amounts of sulfates and chlorides, which supported this effect. Now the rivers of mud were heading down the mountain.

articleEn: The four lahars, formed from melted ice and rock, came down the volcano's slopes. Further along they split into six river valleys. Their average speed was about 60 kilometres per hour. One source says 50 kilometres per hour, so estimates differ, but the speed was very high either way. Along the way they picked up soil, rocks and plants, and once in the valleys the lahars grew to about four times their volume. In the Gualí River, one lahar reached a maximum width of 50 metres. It was an advancing mix of mud, water, ice and pumice.

Armero, 48 kilometres from the volcano, lay in the Lagunilla River valley. That night its power was out and its radios were silent. At 9:45 p.m., civil defense officials in Ibagué and Murillo tried to warn Armero's authorities but could not make contact. Later they heard the Armero authorities talking among themselves. Some heard the mayor saying on ham radio that the danger did not look great.

At about 11:30 p.m., the first lahar hit Armero. People in the town suddenly saw a huge rush of water and heard a loud roar from the direction of the mountain. Many took it for an ordinary flood. But the lahar came in three big waves and was about 30 metres deep. According to one source, the first wave moved at 12 metres per second and lasted 10 to 20 minutes. The second wave was slower and continued for about 30 minutes. After the third big wave, the whole sequence lasted about 2 hours. By then 85 percent of Armero was buried in mud.

Armero's population was 28,700. According to sources, three quarters of them died, and only a quarter survived. Another lahar came down the Chinchiná River valley and reached the Caldas town of Chinchiná. About 1,800 people died there and 400 houses were destroyed.

Now consider the total losses. According to most sources, more than 23,000 people died, about 5,000 were injured and 5,000 houses were destroyed. The destruction spread across 13 settlements. About 230,000 people were affected, and about 20,000 became refugees. Death-toll figures differ between sources. Some give more than 20,000 dead in Armero, and a total of 22,000, 23,000 or 25,000. It was the second deadliest volcanic disaster of the 20th century, behind only the 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée. It was also the deadliest lahar in history, and Colombia's biggest natural disaster. Today it is remembered as the Armero tragedy. But the morning after the disaster was another chapter of the story. When did help arrive, and how did one surviving child become the focus of the world's attention during the wait?

articleEn: The scene in Armero on the morning of 14 November is hard to describe. The whole town lay under grey mud. Relief workers took twelve hours to reach Armero. In many places the mud was up to 4.6 metres deep, and walking on it was almost impossible. In addition, the highway and several bridges had been destroyed by the lahars. The roads were blocked, and the journey of help was slow.

Armero's own hospital was gone too. So helicopters took the injured to nearby hospitals. Temporary triage stations were set up in Lerida, Guayabal and Mariquita, but they were soon overwhelmed by the number of patients. The rest were sent to hospitals in Ibagué. These clinics held 1,244 patients in total, and 150 of them died of infection or related complications. According to sources, if antibiotics had been easily available and treatment better, many of them might have survived. The world also came to help. The United States gave more than 1 million dollars and sent 12 helicopters, and 24 other countries also contributed in total.

But there was another story at the same time. Thirteen-year-old Omayra Sánchez was trapped in the rubble of her house. Her father and aunt died that night, while her brother survived. Rescue teams saw that her legs were trapped in the debris. The problem in trying to free her was that every time they pulled, the surrounding water rose. So a tire was put on her to support her. Even in these conditions Omayra kept her courage. She sang, drank a soda, and even gave an interview to a journalist. A pump arrived later, but her legs were trapped in such a way that she could not be freed without cutting them, and no surgical equipment was available.

About 60 hours later, at about 10:05 a.m. on 16 November, Omayra died. According to sources, the cause was probably gangrene or hypothermia. A photograph of her last hours was taken by Frank Fournier, who had reached Bogotá on 15 November. It became the 1986 World Press Photo of the Year. Some people called Fournier a vulture. He replied that the story had to be told, and that he was glad people had reacted. He also said the photograph helped raise aid from around the world. Defense Minister Miguel Uribe said he understood the criticism of the rescue, but that Colombia was an undeveloped country without such equipment.

A week later, the search was nearly over. Officially 22,540 deaths were recorded, 3,300 people were missing, and 20,000 had lost their homes. For the survivors the hardship did not end. According to one study, they faced anxiety and depression, and psychological support was given only at the start. So whose responsibility was all this? In the next section we look for the answer.

articleEn: So who was to blame? First, scientists could not say exactly when the eruption would happen. And the authorities were not willing to take expensive precautions without a clear and immediate danger. So the decision to evacuate was not easy. The volcano's last big eruption had been more than 140 years earlier. That is why people found it hard to believe in the danger and called it the Sleeping Lion.

A hazard map existed, but it reached people poorly. According to Henry Villegas, it faced strong opposition from economic interests. The map printed in El Espectador had no scale and no key to its colours. Armero was in the green zone, which was wrongly taken to be safe. The Colombian Congress accused scientific and civil defense institutions of scaremongering, so those who spoke of the danger were the ones criticised. Armero's mayor, Ramon Rodriguez, kept warning officials for months. He called the volcano a time bomb, but only one congressman asked about the situation.

On the evening of 13 November the storm stopped what efforts remained. The power went out, communication broke down, and the evacuation order could not actually reach Armero. Later, when scientists looked at the seismograph data, they found many long-period earthquakes in the final hours. In the words of Bernard Chouet, the volcano was screaming, in effect, that it was about to blow. But the scientists studying the volcano at the time could not read this signal.

The country's attention was divided as well. After the Palace of Justice siege of 6 November, the government and army were busy with a guerrilla campaign. After the disaster, anger erupted. At a mass funeral in Ibagué, a banner read: "The volcano didn't kill 22,000 people. The government killed them." Lawmakers campaigned for the resignation of governor Eduardo Alzate Garcia. But the question of responsibility did not end with any one person.

The damage from the disaster was estimated at about one billion dollars, roughly 2 percent of Colombia's GNP in 1985. It was an event in which science, administrative decisions, weather and wrong estimates all collided in a single night. So did Colombia learn anything from it? And how dangerous is Nevado del Ruiz today? That is the next question.

articleEn: After Armero, Colombia created a special agency in 1987, the Oficina Nacional para la Atención de Desastres, to prevent such a disaster from happening again. It was later renamed Dirección de Prevención y Atención de Desastres, the Directorate for Disaster Prevention and Preparedness. Today the system runs under the National Unit for Management of Disasters Risk. All Colombian cities were required to do prevention planning. By law, every Colombian county has a territorial plan, which includes mapping natural hazards and rules for building permits. In 1989 Nevado del Ruiz erupted again, and about 2,300 people living along five nearby rivers were evacuated.

In the United States, the USGS created the Volcano Crisis Assistance Team in 1986 and also set up the Volcano Disaster Assistance Program. Before the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo, these bodies helped move about 75,000 people out of the area. Lessons from Armero also led to a lahar warning system for Mount Rainier, and the USGS has installed warning sirens in Pierce County, Washington. On Mount Ruapehu, New Zealand set up a similar system, which gave timely notice of the lahar that came on 18 March 2007. At Pinatubo, a system of rain gauges and acoustic flow monitors operates, and it helped save hundreds of lives.

But the danger has not gone away. It is estimated that 500,000 people are at risk in the Combeima, Chinchiná, Coello-Toche and Guali valleys, and 100,000 of them are at high risk. According to sources, melting of just 10 percent of the ice could produce a mudflow equal to the Armero lahar, which could reach 100 km in a few hours. In 2012 the alert went to Red and an eruption occurred on 2 July. In March 2023, when seismic activity rose, the alert was raised to Orange and people were evacuated. In June 2023, without any eruption, the alert came back down to Yellow. So the volcano is still under constant watch. In October 2022, the IUGS included it among 100 geological heritage sites, because it is one of the best-studied volcanoes in the world and a model of volcanic risk management.

The town of Armero no longer exists. In its place is a memorial with crosses and a small monument to Omayra. About a year later, Pope John Paul II flew over Armero and declared the site holy land. The story lives on in books, films and music as well. An Isabel Allende short story, the 1999 film Soplo de vida and the 2017 film Armero are examples. In 2008, thousands of people were evacuated during the eruption of Nevado del Huila, because volcanologists feared it might become another Nevado del Ruiz. Armero's name has become a symbol of danger.

It reminds us that receiving a warning is not enough; it must also be taken seriously. So the question is still the same. The next time a volcano, a scientist or a hazard map warns us, will we listen? If you found this story important, please like and subscribe. Friends, we will meet again with the next story.

shorts.titleEn: The Report That Warned of Lahars Weeks Before Armero
shorts.text: کیا ایک رپورٹ نے ہفتوں پہلے خطرے کی گھنٹی بجا دی تھی؟ 22 October 1985 کو ایک Italian volcanological mission نے رپورٹ دی۔ ٹیم نے Arenas crater کے fumaroles سے gas کے samples لیے تھے۔ ان میں carbon dioxide اور sulfur dioxide ملی ہوئی تھیں۔ اس کا مطلب تھا کہ magma سیدھا سطح کے ماحول میں gas چھوڑ رہا ہے۔ رپورٹ کے مطابق lahars کا خطرہ بہت زیادہ تھا۔ اس میں local authorities کے لیے کچھ آسان preparedness techniques بھی تھیں۔ پھر نومبر میں activity دوبارہ بڑھ گئی۔ magma سطح کے قریب آ رہا تھا، اور gases میں sulfur dioxide بڑھ رہی تھی۔ تو کیا ان نشانیوں کو سنجیدگی سے لیا گیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya ek report ne hafton pehle khatre ki ghanti baja di thi? 22 October 1985 ko ek Italian volcanological mission ne report di. Team ne Arenas crater ke fumaroles se gas ke samples liye thay. In mein carbon dioxide aur sulfur dioxide mili hui thin. Is ka matlab tha ke magma seedha satah ke mahol mein gas chhor raha hai. Report ke mutabiq lahars ka khatra bohat zyada tha. Is mein local authorities ke liye kuch aasan preparedness techniques bhi thin. Phir November mein activity dobara barh gayi. magma satah ke qareeb aa raha tha, aur gases mein sulfur dioxide barh rahi thi. To kya in nishaniyon ko sanjeedgi se liya gaya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
An Italian volcanological mission reported very high lahar risk on 22 October 1985, weeks before the Nevado del Ruiz eruption.
This short looks at the gas samples and the warning signs.

shorts.titleEn: Ash Fell Over Armero, and People Were Told to Stay Calm
shorts.text: 13 November 1985 کی دوپہر، لوگوں کو کہا گیا کہ پریشان نہ ہوں۔ تقریباً 3 بجے Ruiz سے کالی راکھ کے ستون اٹھنے لگے۔ local civil defense director کو فوراً بتایا گیا۔ اس نے INGEOMINAS سے رابطہ کیا، جس نے کہا کہ علاقہ خالی کرایا جائے۔ مگر شام کو راکھ گرنا بند ہوئی تو local officials، جن میں town کے priest بھی تھے، لوگوں سے کہنے لگے کہ پرسکون رہیں اور گھروں کے اندر جائیں۔ پھر ایک طوفان آیا۔ Ibagué کی Red Cross نے evacuation کا کہا، مگر بجلی کے مسائل کی وجہ سے اس پر عمل نہ ہو سکا۔ رات 9:45 بجے Ibagué اور Murillo کے officials نے Armero سے رابطے کی کوشش کی، مگر رابطہ نہ ہو سکا۔ آگے کیا ہوا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: 13 November 1985 ki dopahar, logon ko kaha gaya ke pareshan na hon. Taqriban 3 baje Ruiz se kali raakh ke sutoon uthne lage. local civil defense director ko fauran bataya gaya. Us ne INGEOMINAS se rabta kiya, jis ne kaha ke ilaqa khali karaya jaye. Magar sham ko raakh girna band hui to local officials, jin mein town ke priest bhi thay, logon se kehne lage ke pursukoon rahein aur gharon ke andar jayen. Phir ek toofan aaya. Ibagué ki Red Cross ne evacuation ka kaha, magar bijli ke masail ki wajah se is par amal na ho saka. Raat 9:45 baje Ibagué aur Murillo ke officials ne Armero se rabte ki koshish ki, magar rabta na ho saka. Aage kya hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 13 November 1985 ash fell near Nevado del Ruiz, residents were told to stay calm, and a storm cut communications.
This short shows how an evacuation order never reached Armero.

shorts.titleEn: The Hazard Map That Showed Armero in the 'Safe' Zone
shorts.text: ایک نقشہ جس نے Armero کو محفوظ دکھایا۔ کیسے؟ Nevado del Ruiz کے لیے hazard map تیار ہوا تھا۔ مگر El Espectador میں چھپے map پر scale نہیں تھا۔ colours تو تھے، لیکن ان کی کوئی key نہیں تھی۔ Armero green zone میں تھا، جسے غلطی سے سب سے محفوظ سمجھا گیا۔ Henry Villegas کے مطابق map کو economic interests کی سخت مخالفت کا سامنا کرنا پڑا۔ دوسری طرف Colombian Congress نے scientific اور civil defense agencies پر scaremongering کی تنقید کی۔ لوگ آتش فشاں کو Sleeping Lion کہتے تھے، کیونکہ اس کا آخری بڑا eruption 140 سال سے زیادہ پہلے ہوا تھا۔ تو کیا خطرے کی بات مان لی گئی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek naqsha jis ne Armero ko mehfooz dikhaya. Kaise? Nevado del Ruiz ke liye hazard map tayyar hua tha. Magar El Espectador mein chhape map par scale nahin tha. colours to thay, lekin un ki koi key nahin thi. Armero green zone mein tha, jise ghalti se sab se mehfooz samjha gaya. Henry Villegas ke mutabiq map ko economic interests ki sakht mukhalifat ka samna karna pada. Doosri taraf Colombian Congress ne scientific aur civil defense agencies par scaremongering ki tanqeed ki. Log aatish fishan ko Sleeping Lion kehte thay, kyunke is ka aakhri bara eruption 140 saal se zyada pehle hua tha. To kya khatre ki baat maan li gayi? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
A hazard map printed in El Espectador had no scale or colour key, and Armero sat in the green zone.
This short explains why the warning failed to land before the 1985 disaster.
